html:
Hitchiti was a tribal town of the Southeastern Woodlands, in what is now Georgia and Alabama. Its people spoke the Hitchiti language, a Muskogean tongue shared with several neighbouring towns.

Hitchiti first appears as one of the towns of the Apalachicola Province on the Chattahoochee River, heirs of the Mississippian chiefdoms that Hernando de Soto met in 1540. Soon after 1690 these towns moved east to Ochese Creek, the modern Ocmulgee River, to be near English traders from Carolina. After the Yamasee War of 1715 they moved back to the Chattahoochee.

There Hitchiti became one of the Lower Towns of the Muscogee Creek confederacy, keeping its own language inside a larger Creek world. Hitchiti speakers also moved south into Florida and helped form the Seminole; the Mikasuki language of the Miccosukee is close kin to Hitchiti. In the 1830s most Hitchiti were forced west on the Trail of Tears to what is now Oklahoma.
